newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN urges Western Europe not to deport Bosnians.
newsitem.headline: UN urges Western Europe not to deport Bosnians.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency on Friday urged Western European countries not to deport Bosnians who were unable to return to their homes, describing the situation as "potentially explosive" in some Serb-held areas.
Spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole said the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) estimated up to one in three of returnees form Europe could not go home.
Increasing numbers of Bosnians from Germany and Austria have streamed across the border with Croatia during the summer months, but many only find accommodation in reception centres.
"We are concerned however, about those who have been advised to leave by their host countries in Europe, but are unable to return to their home areas," O'Toole told a news briefing.
"We strongly request the European host countries not to deport those who cannot go back to their home areas," she added.
O'Toole said that Bosnian Serb authorities were blocking returnes of ethnic minorities -- Moslems and Croats -- to their territory. She called it a "definite threat to peace".
"We have a potentially explosive situation developing in some areas where local authorities are openly relocating those who cannot return to the Serb-controlled territory.
"We don't want people forced back when there is nowhere for them to go and where the situation is explosive," she said.
Germany has only deported about 400 Bosnians, UNHCR said.
But the UNHCR spokeswoman said: "German authorities do not necessarily want people to stay on. That is clear to people."

Tens of thousands of refugees who fled the civil war in former Yugoslavia have returned home as a result of pressure from cash-strapped German states, according to official data released in Bonn last Tuesday.
More than one-fifth of the 323,000 Bosnians who came to Germany during the 43-month war in the Balkans have gone back, officials from 16 state interior ministries said.

Despite widespread international criticism, the states began forcibly repatriating refugees late last year after efforts to encourage voluntary returns failed. The pressure to leave or face deportation apparently prompted many to go on their own.

A Reuters survey of state governments found that about 65,000 refugees have since left Germany and about 408 have been forcibly deported. About half of those sent against their will had been convicted of crimes in Germany.
